pr_title: winkernel proxier cache HNS data to improve syncProxyRules performance

#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug
<!--
Add one of the following kinds:
/kind bug
/kind cleanup
/kind documentation
/kind feature

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Resolves issues with proxy rules taking a long time to be synced on Windows. This PR reduces the number of expensive calls into HNS for each rule sync cycle and improves the overall proxier performance on Windows.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109162

This addresses the issue of failing service connectivity after a new Windows node has joined a cluster by reducing the time it takes to sync rules needed to reach desired state. During testing, we can see that time taken by kube-proxy on Windows to complete creation of **2000 services of type ClusterIP** on a Node with ~**5000 remote endpoints** and **15 local endpoints/pods**, is reduced as follows:
|  Winkernel proxier                                    | Windows Server 2019 | Windows Server 2022 |
|---------------------------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Without improvements                               | 114 minutes         | 192 minutes         |
| With improvements                                | 110 minutes         | 10 minutes          |
| With improvements + OS updates (shipping separately) | 22 minutes          | 1 minute         |

**NOTE:** The last row is the performance after applying the changes on a Node with an OS update installed, which is shipping separately through Windows Servicing channels. 

**Environment Details:** The node used to test these changes was a Hyper-V VM with 8vCPU cores and 32GB RAM.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

issue_context.title: Delay in processing HNS LB policies on kube-proxy start on Windows nodes results in unreachable services
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

When starting windows nodes with a high number of HNS LB policies/rules on the cluster, there is a delay in processing them. This leaves services unreachable during the delay, which takes about half a minute per policy. This can be substatial given enough rules.

This occurs when restarting kube-proxy and rebooting the host. Once the system does reach a state where all the policylists are processed, incremental updates to the services are handled fine (ie. endpoint changes).

### What did you expect to happen?

HNS policies should not cause a large delay for Windows nodes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

With a large number of HNS policies in place, restart kube-proxy on a Windows node.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

There are more details on timing in the fix that @daschott opened https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109124

When doing a sync of Services on a new node joining the cluster, the HNS is queried for state on every endpoint in a service which is expensive. When iterating over thousands of services, this can take hours (!).  

The fix proposed by @daschott gets the HNS state once per sync instead of each time. This plus a fix in Windows OS the sync is reduced to mins in WS 2019 and ~1 min in WS 2022.

@daschott @jsturtevant 
For the Windows OS fix mentioned, do you know when will it arrive at Windows Server 2019?

review_comments: add length of endpoints to struct
this will always be `nil` now, can simplify to `newHnsEndpoint := queriedEndpoints[ep.IP()]` and remove `var newHnsEndpoint *endpointsInfo` from a few lines above

Why is the endpoint being stored it by ip and hnsid in the same map?  The `getAllEndpointsByNetwork` function only stores it by ip when first called above.  We will be doubling the storage for large sets of endpoints?
This only happens on overlay networks?
+1, suggest to use another map to cache the (endpoint IP, endpoint ID) pair.

I see now that the new `getAllEndpointsByNetwork` is storing by `hsnID` and `ip` but I don't see a reason why.  There is only one spot that the `queriedEndpoints` is looked up by `hnsId` and it is followed immediately by a look up for `ip`.  I think we should just store and look up by `ip` or `hsnId` unless there is a reason needed for looking up by both, which isn't immediately apparent.

Thanks for your suggestion! Out of an abundance of caution, I did not want to change any of the logic in syncProxyRules that was used and wanted to avoid doing any optimizations outside of caching HNS information. 

But I agree this should be safe to remove. In my latest commit, I have removed the storage by endpoint ID, and am storing by endpoint IP only. Thank you!

After more deliberation with @sbangari, I will revert back to query endpoints by ID, and thereby double the size of the map again. Unfortunately it appears there is a bug in Windows Server 2019 that could sometimes cause 2 endpoints to be populated with the same IP address, and there is fear of this potentially causing issues if we only query by IP address and remove the call to query by ID. Doubling the size of the map is acceptable for now and we will clean this up instead in the next round of optimizations coming in 2-3 months, after we had sufficient time for testing and validation.
Out of abundance of caution, I have reverted back to the old behavior to ensure nothing breaks on Windows Server 2019.

Why is this queried here and by ip right after?  This looks valid only in the overlay scenario and only due to previous way this worked. For any endpoints that already exist is would be found by IP.  (similiar to comment above)
